story.e: David was living in peace at last. He lived in his own house of cedar, the wars were over, and the ark of the covenant was in Jerusalem — but only in a tent. That would not let him rest. He called the prophet Nathan and said: “Look, I live in a house of cedar, while God’s ark is in a tent.” Nathan first answered: “Do what you wish, for the Lord is with you.” But that very night the Lord spoke to Nathan. The message was quite different from what they expected. The Lord said: “Are you the one to build me a house? I have not lived in a house since I brought Israel out of Egypt: I have travelled with my people in a tent. Did I ever ask anyone to build me a house of cedar?” Then he went on, and here everything turned around: “I took you from the flock to be the leader of my people. I was with you wherever you went. I will make your name great. And now I tell you: you will not build me a house; I will build you a house.” God turned the sentence around. David wanted to give God a house; God promised David a family, a future, permanence. He also said that David’s son would build the temple, and that God would be his father: if he sinned, he would discipline him, but he would not withdraw his love as he had from Saul. The greatest sentence came at the end: “Your house and your kingdom will last for ever.” When David heard this he did not celebrate or boast. He went in, sat down before the Lord, and asked: “Who am I, Lord, and what is my family, that you have brought me this far?” Then he gave thanks that God had not chosen him for his greatness but out of his own goodness. At the end of the chapter David asks for exactly what he has just been given: “Bless your servant’s house, that it may last for ever before you.” So in this chapter David did not give God something; he learned to receive what he was given.
story.m: David was living in peace at last. He lived in his own palace of cedar, and the Lord had given him rest from all his enemies around him. One day he said to the prophet Nathan: “Look, I live in a house of cedar, while God’s ark sits among tent curtains.” Nathan answered the king: “Do all that is in your heart, for the Lord is with you!” That same night, however, the word of the Lord came to Nathan: “Go and tell my servant David: Are you the one to build me a house to live in? I have not lived in a house from the day I brought the Israelites out of Egypt until now; I have moved about in a tent and a dwelling. Wherever I went among the Israelites, did I ever say to any of Israel’s leaders whom I commanded to shepherd my people: why have you not built me a house of cedar?” Then everything turned around. “Now therefore tell my servant David: Thus says the Lord of Hosts: I took you from the flock, from following the sheep, to be prince over my people Israel. I have been with you wherever you went, and I have cut off all your enemies before you. I will make your name great, like the names of the greatest on earth. I will provide a place for my people Israel and plant them, so that they may live in their own place and wander no more. I will give you rest from all your enemies. The Lord also declares to you that he will build you a house. When your life is over and you rest with your fathers, I will raise up your offspring who comes from you, and I will establish his kingdom. He will build a house for my name, and I will establish his royal throne for ever. I will be a father to him, and he will be my son. If he commits sin, I will discipline him with the rod of men and with human blows, but I will not withdraw my love from him as I withdrew it from Saul, whom I rejected before you. Your house and your kingdom will endure for ever before me; your throne will be firm for ever.” Nathan told David everything he had heard. Then King David went in, sat down before the Lord and asked: “Who am I, Lord God, and what is my family, that you have brought me this far? And as if this were too little in your sight, Lord God, you have also spoken of the distant future of your servant’s house. Is this how a man usually speaks, Lord God? What more can David say to you? For you know your servant! According to your word and the purpose of your heart you have done all this great thing, and revealed it to your servant. Therefore you are great, Lord God: there is none like you, and there is no God but you. Who is like your people Israel, the one nation on earth for whom God went out to redeem for himself? Now therefore, Lord God, keep for ever the word you have spoken about your servant and his house, and do as you have said! For you, Lord of Hosts, God of Israel, have given your servant this revelation: I will build you a house. That is why your servant has the courage to pray to you like this. Now then, be gracious, and bless your servant’s house, that it may last for ever before you! For what you, Lord God, bless will be blessed for ever.” So in this chapter David did not give God something; he learned to receive what he was given.
story.h: This is one of the Bible’s most important chapters, and it is worth reading very slowly, because almost everything that matters turns on the reversal of a single word. That word is “house”. At the start of the chapter David says: I will build God a house — he means a temple. In the middle of the chapter God turns the same word back: you will not build me a house, I will build you a house — and here “house” means family, descendants, permanence. The wordplay is not linguistic cleverness but the teaching itself: while David wants to give, God gives; while David wants to build, God builds. Four things are worth looking at separately. The first is Nathan’s mistake. The prophet Nathan first approves the plan: “do all that is in your heart, for the Lord is with you”. That is well-meant advice and religiously impeccable — it simply did not come from God. That very night God corrects it. It is rare and very brave that the Bible preserved this: even a prophet does not stand in for God, and a true man of God can go back and correct himself. The second is God’s question: “did I ever ask anyone to build me a house of cedar?” God does not depend on anything a human can give. This is not rejection but a setting-straight: religious zeal very easily turns into the thought that God needs us. The third is David’s past: “I took you from the flock”. God begins the review exactly where part 4 of this module began. David’s whole life fits into one sentence, and it is not about his own talent. The fourth is the size of the promise. The word “for ever” here reaches beyond David’s family: the later prophets and the New Testament go back to this chapter when they speak of a messianic promise. It is worth noticing too that the promise contains the possibility of discipline — “I will discipline him if he sins” — but not of withdrawal. God does not give a promise that would make sin not sin; he gives one that does not break even in the face of sin. Finally it is worth watching David’s answer, because that is the measure of the chapter. He does not say “I deserved it”, nor “I will build the temple anyway”. He sits down and asks: “Who am I?” That question is one of the most mature sentences in the whole Bible: not cringing modesty but the mark of clear sight. David understands exactly that what has happened is not his own achievement, and that is precisely why he can be thankful for it.

verse.text: Your house and your kingdom will endure for ever.
